analysis.one_liner: Creates a universal government health insurance program covering everyone with no deductibles or copays.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 14 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on April 10, 2019 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace private health insurance, employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and the ACA exchanges with a single national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services. Every U.S. resident would be enrolled automatically and could use any participating doctor or hospital, with no deductibles or copays — only up to $200 a year in possible prescription drug charges for higher-income people. Coverage would include dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care, and private insurers could sell only supplemental policies, not the main coverage. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed coverage regardless of employment, income, or health status, with free choice of any participating provider and no cost-sharing except a possible annual prescription cap of $200 (waived below 200% of poverty) [S2][S3]. People currently skipping care because of deductibles, the uninsured, and those needing dental, vision, hearing, or long-term care — benefits most private plans limit — would gain the most [S2][S3]. The bill also bans balance billing and ends insurers' ability to deny or limit care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured and underinsured

how_it_helps.text: Establishes automatic, universal enrollment: every U.S. resident is entitled to benefits, enrolled at birth or on establishing residency, with a Universal Medicare card
Eliminates deductibles, coinsurance, and copays for covered services; the only exception is prescription drugs, capped at $200 per year and free for households below 200% of the poverty line
Covers a broader package than typical private insurance, including dental, vision, hearing, mental health and substance use treatment, prescription drugs, and home- and community-based long-term care
Lets patients use any qualified provider with no networks, prohibits balance billing, and forbids discrimination based on race, sex, gender identity, disability, or pregnancy

Ends the current system's biggest sources of bankruptcy and lost coverage: private insurers may sell only supplemental coverage, employers may not offer duplicative plans, and the ACA exchanges, Medicare, Medicaid, and FEHB as they exist would be folded into the new program
Requires HHS to negotiate prescription drug prices and run a formulary that steers toward generics

Includes a transition: children covered within one year, a Medicare buy-in dropping to age 35 within three years, and elimination of Medicare deductibles and the disability waiting period along the way

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the entire system through a new Universal Medicare Trust Fund; the bill text contains no tax title, instead appropriating existing federal health spending and revenue 'attributable to' other amendments, leaving the actual financing mechanism unspecified [S3]. Private health insurers would lose their core business, since selling coverage duplicating the program would be unlawful [S2][S3]. Employers would stop paying employee premiums, but the cost would reappear in taxes. Hospitals and doctors would be paid under Medicare-style fee schedules rather than higher commercial rates, with no balance billing allowed [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, private insurers, and providers paid Medicare rates

drawbacks.text: The bill text contains no financing mechanism: the Universal Medicare Trust Fund is filled by appropriations and revenue 'attributable to' amendments that do not actually impose taxes, so the question of how a program of this size gets paid for is left entirely open

It outlaws private coverage that duplicates program benefits, ending the employer-sponsored insurance that roughly most working-age Americans rely on today and eliminating the primary business of the health insurance industry; the bill sets aside only up to 1% of the budget for five years to assist displaced insurance-system workers

Providers would be paid under Medicare fee schedules and barred from balance billing, meaning hospitals and physicians could no longer charge privately insured patients higher rates — a real strain that opponents of single-payer plans routinely cite

Full implementation takes four years, with children covered after one year and adults phased in through a premium-based transitional buy-in, so people would live under a patchwork of old and new rules during the transition

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the largest single expansion of guaranteed health coverage ever proposed in Congress: everyone covered, no deductibles or copays, dental and long-term care included, and no networks or balance billing. The cost is equally large and largely unaddressed in the bill itself — it never specifies the taxes that would replace the roughly $3.5 trillion Americans and their employers now pay in premiums and out-of-pocket costs, and it would eliminate the private insurance market and its jobs while paying providers Medicare rates. A serious version of this bill needed a financing title and a provider-transition plan; this one had neither, which is part of why it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, so it never came to the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the Medicare for All Act of 2019 on April 10, 2019, joined by 14 Democratic senators including several running for president that year
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance
No further action of any kind appears in the record — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, pharmaceutical manufacturers, and employers keep the existing employer-based, multi-payer system intact; nothing changed, so the status quo's beneficiaries are better off because the bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and drug makers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or the independent Sanders; no Republican ever signed on, and the committee controlled by Republicans took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to sell coverage duplicating program benefits, leaving insurers only supplemental policies — the end of their core business. Their preservation depends on the status quo the bill would have replaced.
HHS would negotiate drug prices annually and run a formulary that pushes prescribing toward generics, threatening the industry's pricing power in the world's most profitable drug market.
Providers would gain a guaranteed payer for every patient and an end to unpaid bills, but would be paid Medicare fee schedules instead of higher commercial rates and could not balance-bill patients.

Employers could no longer offer primary health coverage (and would lose ERISA continuation-coverage duties), shifting a major benefit cost off their books — but the expense would return through the taxes financing the program.
Workers' comp carriers would have to reimburse the Universal Medicare Program for medical costs of work-related injuries, narrowing their medical-benefit business.
